newsitem.title: CUBA: Susie Maroney hopes technology will help Cuba swim.
newsitem.headline: Susie Maroney hopes technology will help Cuba swim.

text.p: Australian marathon swimmer Susie Maroney, who will try to swim from Cuba to the United States this week, is hoping a combination of satellite technology and good old fashioned willpower will help her beat the treacherous currents of the Florida Straits.
It will be the second attempt by the 22-year-old swimmer to cover the 58 miles (93 km) from Havana to Key West.
In her first attempt last year, she endured a storm and unexpected currents and was plucked from the water 12 miles (19 km) short of the Florida Keys after 38 hours and 30 minutes.
Weather permitting, Maroney intends to dive off from the Havana shoreline early on Friday morning to start her swim.
Maroney hoped Cuban President Fidel Castro might come to see her off at the start of her swim. "That will give me motivation," she told a news conference in Havana on Tuesday.

This year, her team of navigators and family members, including her mother and brother, will be consulting satellite photos to try to plot the best course through shifting ocean currents, a technological aid they did not have last year.

"I think this will really help, especially when you're getting into currents you might have to fight. If we can find a hole where you don't have to do that, it's going to make a big difference," Maroney said.

But her zig-zagging route meant she would actually swim a lot further than the straight line distance, maybe even as much as 125 miles (200 km), she said. She expected to spend between 40 and 45 hours in the water, resting every hour by treading water and taking in food and fluids.

The strong Gulf Stream currents will initially work to her advantage, pushing her in the general direction of the Keys as they whip eastward around the southern tip of Florida. Then she will have to cut across the current or be swept parallel with the island chain.

Maroney said that despite the technical gadgetry like the staellite photos and a specially designed shark cage, in the end a swim of this distance became a simple battle of the human will. "It's pretty much my mental attitude," she said.

To help keep her in good spirits, her accompanying crew will play music, shout encouragement and feed her hot coffee, chocolate and baby food during her rest stops. Maroney said prolonged immersion in sea water made her throat swell and baby food slipped down easier.
She lost 24 pounds (11 kg) during the last swim and needed to force herself to take food.
But the swimmer, who has been training for six hours a day for most of the last year, seemed determined. "The challenge is still there...I have to keep trying" she said.
"I enjoy being out in the ocean, testing my body, pushing it to its limits," she added.
Last year, she swam for periods outside her shark cage and at one point was accompanied by a sperm whale.

The swimmer and her team were waiting for calm sea conditions to be able to start. Two camera crews will follow her swim on accompanying boats, one from the United States and the other from Australia.
